newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia sees no need for monetary policy changes.
newsitem.headline: Croatia sees no need for monetary policy changes.

text.p: Croatia's central bank said on Thursday there was no need to radically change its restrictive monetary policy, but promised to ease its tight reins over time to aid the ex-Yugoslav republic's economic recovery.
"Why change a winning horse?" governor Marko Skreb told a news conference.
Croatia is negotiating a new loan with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to support ongoing reforms, but a deal has been held up by delays in the government's budget plans.

The government launched a tough stabilisation package in October 1993 to fight war-induced hyperinflation. Since then, inflation has run at an annual average of about one percent. It stood at 3.1 percent year-on-year in September.

Introduced at 3.70 to the German mark, the kuna has firmed to around 3.55, prompting repeated complaints from exporters who are struggling to establish new markets to compensate for lost trade with other ex-Yugoslav republics after Croatia gained independence in 1991.

Average interest rates have fallen to about 21 percent from 30 percent this spring but Skreb warned further steps were needed to rehabilitate the still-fragile banking sector and troubled state-owned companies.
He said this year's inflation rate could fall below last year's two percent, adding the exchange rate was also likely to remain stable with fluctuations kept to a narrow range.
"If positive developments in the overall economic and fiscal sphere continue, that will leave more freedom for monetary policy," he said.

To help Croatia's cash-strapped economy get back on its feet, the bank was weighing further cuts in its reserve requirement, which has already fallen to 35.85 percent on kuna deposits from 41 percent earlier this year.
A provision obliging commercial banks to deposit abroad more than 50 percent of their foreign currency liabilities would also be reconsidered, Skreb said.
He added the central bank would step up its drive to introduce open market operations as a way to a better control money supply growth.
However, he vowed the central bank would keep a close eye on price and kuna stability as a key condition for sustainable growth. Wage increases also had to be watched to keep a lid on inflation.
The central bank, matching the government's expectations, has forecast economic growth of no less than seven percent this year, up from around three percent in 1995.
Strong recovery in the service sector, led by tourism, transport and trade, should make up for weak industrial growth, the central bank said, mirroring recent predictions by the IMF.
Although on an upward trend, industrial output growth in the first eight months of the year was a meagre one percent.
"We are operating with a (1996) GDP estimate in the region of 100 billion kuna. There are some indications it may be considerably higher," Skreb said.
